slides.narration: Namaste! The two rows printed separately at the bottom of the periodic table are the inner transition elements. The lanthanoids are found in the magnets of electric motors, the phosphors of screens and the flints of lighters. In this part we study how their electrons are arranged, why they are so alike, and the famous lanthanoid contraction.

slides.heading: Lanthanoids and actinoids: position
slides.body_md: In the **f-block**, electrons enter an **(n−2)f** subshell. The **lanthanoids** are the fourteen elements **cerium (58) to lutetium (71)** that follow lanthanum and fill **4f**; the **actinoids**, thorium (90) to lawrencium (103), fill **5f**. Lanthanum and actinium are usually studied with them. Lanthanoids belong to group 3, period 6.

visual.alt: Table of the two f-block series

slides.narration: The f-block has two series of fourteen. The lanthanoids, from cerium to lutetium, follow lanthanum and fill the four f subshell. The actinoids, from thorium to lawrencium, follow actinium and fill five f. Because the f subshell lies two shells inside the outermost one, adding f electrons changes the outer electrons very little, which is why each series is so uniform.

slides.heading: Electronic configurations of the lanthanoids
slides.body_md: General configuration $[\text{Xe}]4f^{1\text{–}14}5d^{0\text{–}1}6s^2$. The 4f and 5d levels are close in energy; a 5d electron appears only in **La, Ce, Gd and Lu**, where it keeps the 4f subshell empty, half-filled or full (Gd 4f⁷5d¹, Lu 4f¹⁴5d¹).

visual.alt: Table of the electronic configurations of selected lanthanoids

slides.narration: All the lanthanoids have two six s electrons outside a xenon core, and their four f subshells fill from one to fourteen. Because four f and five d are close in energy, a five d electron appears only in a few cases, such as gadolinium and lutetium, where it keeps the four f subshell exactly half-filled or completely full.

slides.heading: Worked example: configurations of Ln³⁺ ions
slides.body_md:
**Rule.** To form Ln³⁺, remove the two 6s electrons and then one 5d electron (if present), otherwise one 4f electron.

**Problem.** Write the configurations of Nd³⁺ (Nd = 60), Gd³⁺ (Gd = 64), Tm³⁺ (Tm = 69) and Lu³⁺ (Lu = 71).

**Step 1.** Nd [Xe]4f⁴6s² → Nd³⁺ [Xe]4f³. Gd [Xe]4f⁷5d¹6s² → Gd³⁺ [Xe]4f⁷.

**Step 2.** Tm [Xe]4f¹³6s² → Tm³⁺ [Xe]4f¹². Lu [Xe]4f¹⁴5d¹6s² → Lu³⁺ [Xe]4f¹⁴.

visual.alt: Table of Ln three plus configurations and unpaired electrons

slides.narration: To form a tripositive ion, take away the two six s electrons first, and then a five d electron if there is one; otherwise take a four f electron. Neodymium three plus is four f three. Gadolinium loses its five d electron and keeps a half-filled four f seven. Thulium three plus is four f twelve, and lutetium three plus has a full four f fourteen.

slides.heading: Quick check: Ln³⁺ configuration
slides.body_md: Choose the configuration of a tripositive lanthanoid ion.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remove the two outer s electrons, then a five d electron if there is one, otherwise a four f electron.

slides.heading: Oxidation states
slides.body_md: The **+3** state is common to all lanthanoids (three ionisation enthalpies are balanced by high lattice and hydration enthalpies of Ln³⁺). Some show **+2** or **+4** when this gives an **empty (f⁰), half-filled (f⁷) or full (f¹⁴)** subshell, or is close to it.

visual.alt: Table of lanthanoid ions in the plus two and plus four states

slides.narration: Every lanthanoid forms a plus three ion. The energy spent removing three electrons is repaid by the large lattice and hydration enthalpies of the small, highly charged ion. A few also show plus two or plus four, usually where this gives an empty, half-filled or full four f subshell. But since plus three is the most stable, these ions tend to change back to it.

slides.heading: Worked example: Ce⁴⁺ and Eu²⁺
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Explain why (a) Ce⁴⁺ is a good oxidising agent in aqueous solution, and (b) Eu²⁺ is a good reducing agent. ($E^\circ_{\ce{Ce^4+/Ce^3+}} = +1.74\ \text{V}$; $E^\circ_{\ce{Eu^3+/Eu^2+}} = -0.35\ \text{V}$)

**(a)** Ce⁴⁺ (4f⁰) is stabilised by its noble-gas core, but +3 is the most stable state of cerium, so Ce⁴⁺ readily gains an electron. Its high positive potential confirms this.

**(b)** Eu²⁺ (4f⁷) has a half-filled subshell, but Eu³⁺ is more stable in water, so Eu²⁺ readily loses an electron; the negative potential confirms this.

visual.alt: Flow showing cerium four plus gaining an electron and europium two plus losing an electron to reach the stable plus three state

slides.narration: Cerium four plus has the stable xenon core, which explains why it can exist. But for lanthanoids the plus three state is the most stable, so cerium four plus takes an electron and is a strong oxidising agent, with a large positive electrode potential. Europium two plus has a half-filled four f subshell, yet it gives up an electron easily to become europium three plus, so it acts as a reducing agent.

slides.heading: Quick check: oxidation states
slides.body_md: Decide whether a lanthanoid ion is oxidising or reducing.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember that the plus three state is the most stable, and look for empty, half-filled or full four f subshells.

slides.heading: Colour, magnetism, complexes and alloys
slides.body_md: Many Ln³⁺ ions are **coloured** because of **f–f transitions**; ions with **f⁰** (La³⁺, Ce⁴⁺) or **f¹⁴** (Lu³⁺, Yb²⁺) are colourless. Ions with unpaired f electrons are **paramagnetic**. Lanthanoids form **few complexes** (large ions, low charge density; 4f not available for bonding), mostly with O- and N-donor ligands. **Mischmetall** (about 95% lanthanoid metals, 5% iron, traces of S, C, Ca, Al) is used in lighter flints and in magnesium alloys for shells and bullets.

visual.alt: Table of colours of some tripositive lanthanoid ions

slides.narration: Many lanthanoid ions are coloured, because an f electron absorbs visible light and moves to another f level. Praseodymium three plus is green and neodymium three plus lilac, while lanthanum and lutetium three plus, with empty and full f subshells, are colourless. Lanthanoid ions are large, so they form fewer complexes than the d-block. Mischmetall, mostly lanthanoids with some iron, makes lighter flints.

slides.heading: The lanthanoid contraction
slides.body_md: From La to Lu, atomic and **Ln³⁺ ionic radii decrease steadily**: the **lanthanoid contraction**. **Cause:** each added electron enters the 4f subshell, whose diffuse shape **shields poorly**, so the effective nuclear charge on the outer electrons rises steadily.

visual.alt: Ionic radius of the tripositive lanthanoid ions falling smoothly and steadily from about 103 picometres for lanthanum to about 86 for lutetium
visual.caption: Approximate values; the steady fall is the lanthanoid contraction.

slides.narration: Across the lanthanoids the tripositive ions shrink smoothly, from about one hundred and three picometres for lanthanum to about eighty six for lutetium. Each step adds one proton and one four f electron. The four f orbitals are spread out and shield the outer electrons poorly, so the extra nuclear charge pulls the outer shell a little closer each time. This steady shrinking is the lanthanoid contraction.

slides.heading: Consequences of the lanthanoid contraction
slides.body_md: The contraction cancels the size increase expected on going from the 4d to the 5d series, and makes lanthanoid properties change only very gradually.

rows: 4d and 5d elements of a group have almost the same radius
Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm; Nb and Ta; Mo and W
These pairs have very similar chemistry
Zr and Hf occur together and are very hard to separate
Basic character of Ln(OH)₃ decreases from La to Lu
Smaller Ln³⁺ holds OH⁻ more covalently
Ion exchange or fractional crystallisation needed
Same size as 4d but much heavier (e.g. Os, Ir)

visual.alt: Table of the consequences of the lanthanoid contraction

slides.narration: The lanthanoid contraction reaches beyond the f-block. Elements of the third transition series come after the lanthanoids, and the contraction cancels the extra shell, so pairs such as zirconium and hafnium, or niobium and tantalum, are nearly the same size and almost identical chemically. Within the series, hydroxides become less basic as the ions shrink, and the elements are very hard to separate.

slides.heading: Worked example: using the contraction
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) Arrange La(OH)₃, Gd(OH)₃ and Lu(OH)₃ in order of decreasing basic strength. (b) Explain why the density of hafnium (13.3 g cm⁻³) is nearly double that of zirconium (6.5 g cm⁻³).

**(a)** Ln³⁺ radius: La³⁺ > Gd³⁺ > Lu³⁺. A smaller cation polarises OH⁻ more, so the Ln–OH bond is more covalent and less OH⁻ is released: **La(OH)₃ > Gd(OH)₃ > Lu(OH)₃**.

**(b)** Hf and Zr have almost the same radius (lanthanoid contraction), but Hf (178.5 u) is nearly twice as heavy as Zr (91.2 u), so the same volume holds about twice the mass.

visual.alt: Table relating Ln three plus radius to the basic strength of the hydroxide

slides.narration: For the hydroxides, follow the size of the ion. Lanthanum three plus is largest, so its hydroxide is the most ionic and most basic; lutetium three plus is smallest, holds hydroxide most covalently and gives the least basic hydroxide. For hafnium and zirconium, the atoms are almost the same size, but hafnium is about twice as heavy, so its density is about twice as great.

slides.body_md: Use the lanthanoid contraction to explain a property.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of poor shielding by four f electrons and its effect on size.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Lanthanoids Ce–Lu fill 4f: [Xe]4f¹⁻¹⁴5d⁰⁻¹6s²; 5d¹ only in La, Ce, Gd, Lu.
+3 is the common, most stable state; Ce⁴⁺ and Tb⁴⁺ oxidising, Eu²⁺, Yb²⁺, Sm²⁺ reducing.
Colour from f–f transitions; f⁰ and f¹⁴ colourless; few complexes; mischmetall.
Lanthanoid contraction: steady fall in size from La to Lu due to poor 4f shielding.

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. The lanthanoids fill the four f subshell and all keep two six s electrons. Plus three is their most stable state, with a few plus two and plus four ions that are reducing or oxidising. Their ions are often coloured because of f to f transitions. Poor shielding by four f electrons causes the lanthanoid contraction, which makes zirconium and hafnium twins.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1

For +2 and +4 ions, say whether they are oxidising or reducing and why.
Name two consequences of the contraction with examples.

For unusual oxidation states, say whether the ion is oxidising or reducing and link it to the stability of plus three. Learn two consequences of the contraction with examples, and remember the order for removing electrons when forming a tripositive ion.

decks.title: Inner Transition Elements — Part 2: Reactivity of lanthanoids, and the actinoids
goals: Write the products formed when lanthanoids react with oxygen, hydrogen, halogens, sulphur, nitrogen, carbon, water and acids
Describe the configurations and oxidation states of the actinoids
Compare actinoids with lanthanoids and explain the wider range of actinoid oxidation states

slides.heading: Reactive metals and radioactive cousins
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how lanthanoids react, and how the actinoids differ.

visual.alt: Flow from lanthanoid metals reacting like calcium to plus three compounds and then to the more varied actinoids

slides.narration: The lanthanoids are silvery, reactive metals that tarnish in air and behave rather like calcium. Almost all of their compounds contain the tripositive ion. In this part we write the equations for their reactions with common non-metals and with water, and then meet the actinoids: radioactive, more varied, and the fuel of nuclear power stations.

slides.heading: General reactivity of the lanthanoids
slides.body_md: Lanthanoids are **soft, silvery, highly electropositive metals** ($E^\circ_{\ce{Ln^3+/Ln}}$ about −2.2 to −2.4 V). Early members (La, Ce) are about as reactive as **calcium**; reactivity falls slightly towards Lu as the size decreases. They tarnish quickly in moist air and usually react on heating.

rows: Soft; harder from La to Lu

visual.alt: Table of general properties of lanthanoid metals

slides.narration: Lanthanoid metals are soft and silvery, and they quickly lose their shine in moist air. Their standard electrode potentials are around minus two point three volts, so they are strong reducing agents, rather like calcium. Reactivity falls a little across the series as the atoms become smaller. Most of their reactions with non-metals need heating.

slides.heading: Reactions with non-metals
slides.body_md: Ln = any lanthanoid metal. Products contain Ln³⁺.

visual.alt: Table of reactions of lanthanoid metals with oxygen, hydrogen, halogens, sulphur, nitrogen and carbon

slides.narration: When heated, the lanthanoids combine directly with most non-metals. They burn in oxygen to give oxides of formula Ln two O three, though cerium gives cerium dioxide. With hydrogen they give hydrides, with halogens trihalides, with sulphur sulphides, and with nitrogen nitrides. At very high temperature, about two thousand seven hundred and seventy three kelvin, they combine with carbon to form carbides.

slides.heading: Reactions with water and acids
slides.body_md: Lanthanoids react **slowly with cold water and faster with hot water**, giving the hydroxide and hydrogen. With **dilute acids** they liberate hydrogen.

visual.alt: Table of reactions of lanthanoids with water and dilute acids

slides.narration: Like calcium, the lanthanoids react with water to release hydrogen and form a hydroxide; the reaction is slow in cold water and faster in hot water. With dilute acids, such as hydrochloric acid, they dissolve to give the tripositive salt and hydrogen gas. The hydroxides are ionic and basic, but basicity falls across the series, as we saw in Part 1.

slides.heading: Worked example: writing lanthanoid equations
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write balanced equations for: (a) samarium burning in oxygen; (b) heating gadolinium with sulphur; (c) europium(III) chloride formed from the metal and chlorine; (d) lanthanum heated with carbon to give the dicarbide.

**(a)** $\ce{4Sm + 3O2 -> 2Sm2O3}$

**(b)** $\ce{2Gd + 3S -> Gd2S3}$

**(c)** $\ce{2Eu + 3Cl2 -> 2EuCl3}$

**(d)** $\ce{La + 2C -> LaC2}$

visual.alt: Table of products for the worked example

slides.narration: Start with the formula of the product, using the plus three state: samarium oxide is Sm two O three, gadolinium sulphide Gd two S three, europium chloride EuCl three. Then balance the atoms. Four samarium atoms need three oxygen molecules, two gadolinium atoms need three sulphur atoms, and two europium atoms need three chlorine molecules. Lanthanum and carbon give the dicarbide.

slides.heading: Quick check: lanthanoid reactions
slides.body_md: Predict the product of a lanthanoid reacting with a non-metal or water.
slides.narration: Quick check. Use the plus three state to write the formula of the product.

slides.heading: The actinoids
slides.body_md: Actinoids, **thorium (90) to lawrencium (103)**, fill the **5f** subshell: general configuration $[\text{Rn}]5f^{1\text{–}14}6d^{0\text{–}1}7s^2$. **All are radioactive**; only Th and U occur in significant amounts in nature, and the elements after uranium (**transuranium elements**) are made artificially. There is an **actinoid contraction**, greater than the lanthanoid contraction because 5f electrons shield even more poorly.

visual.alt: Table of configurations of the early actinoids

slides.narration: The actinoids run from thorium to lawrencium and fill the five f subshell. Every one of them is radioactive. Thorium and uranium occur in ores, but the elements beyond uranium, called transuranium elements, are made in nuclear reactors and accelerators, often in tiny amounts. The actinoids also shrink across the series, and this actinoid contraction is even greater than the lanthanoid one.

slides.heading: Oxidation states of the actinoids
slides.body_md: Actinoids show a **much wider range of oxidation states** than lanthanoids. The maximum rises from +4 (Th) to **+7 (Np, Pu)** and then falls; later actinoids are mainly +3. **Reason:** 5f, 6d and 7s levels are **close in energy**, and 5f orbitals extend further out than 4f, so more electrons can take part in bonding.

visual.alt: Highest oxidation state of the early actinoids rising from plus four for thorium to plus seven for neptunium and plutonium, then falling again to plus four for curium and berkelium
visual.caption: Compare: almost every lanthanoid has a highest state of only +3 or +4.

slides.narration: Here is the big difference. Thorium reaches plus four, protactinium plus five, uranium plus six, and neptunium and plutonium plus seven, before the maximum falls again. The five f, six d and seven s levels are very close in energy, and the five f orbitals reach out further than four f, so many more electrons can be used in bonding than in the lanthanoids.

slides.heading: Worked example: uranium oxidation states
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the oxidation state of uranium in (a) UF₆, used to enrich uranium, (b) the uranyl ion UO₂²⁺, and (c) UO₂, nuclear fuel. Which lanthanoid could show the same highest state?

**(a)** $x + 6(-1) = 0$, so $x = +6$.

**(b)** $x + 2(-2) = +2$, so $x = +6$.

**(c)** $x + 2(-2) = 0$, so $x = +4$.

No lanthanoid reaches +6 (the maximum is +4), showing the wider range of the actinoids.

visual.alt: Table of uranium oxidation states in the worked example

slides.narration: Use the usual rules: fluorine minus one, oxygen minus two, and the total equal to the charge. In uranium hexafluoride, uranium is plus six. In the uranyl ion, two oxygens contribute minus four and the ion carries plus two, so uranium is again plus six. In uranium dioxide it is plus four. No lanthanoid gets beyond plus four, which shows how much wider the actinoid range is.

slides.heading: Lanthanoids and actinoids compared
slides.body_md: Both fill f orbitals and both contract across the series, but the **5f orbitals are less shielded and less buried** than 4f.
columns:
**Lanthanoids (4f)**

- Mainly +3; at most +4
- Only promethium radioactive
- Smaller contraction
- Less complex formation
- Hydroxides and oxides basic

**Actinoids (5f)**

- +3 to +7
- All radioactive
- Greater contraction
- Greater complex formation (e.g. UO₂²⁺ complexes)
- Oxides and hydroxides less basic

visual.alt: Table comparing lanthanoids and actinoids

slides.narration: Let us compare the two series side by side. Both fill an f subshell and both contract, but the five f orbitals are less deeply buried. So actinoids show more oxidation states, a larger contraction and a greater tendency to form complexes. Apart from promethium, lanthanoids are not radioactive, whereas every actinoid is, which makes actinoid chemistry difficult to study.

slides.heading: Quick check: actinoids
slides.body_md: Explain a difference between actinoids and lanthanoids.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about how close the five f, six d and seven s levels are in energy.

slides.heading: Uses of f-block elements
slides.body_md: Lanthanoids and actinoids have important modern uses.

rows: Lighter flints; Mg alloy for bullets and shells
Powerful permanent magnets in motors and headphones
Red and green phosphors in screens and lamps
Possible future nuclear fuel (India’s thorium programme)

visual.alt: Table of uses of f-block elements

slides.narration: The f-block elements are part of daily life. Neodymium magnets drive electric vehicle motors and headphones. Europium and terbium compounds give the red and green light in screens and lamps. Cerium oxide polishes glass, and mischmetall makes lighter flints. Uranium and plutonium fuel nuclear reactors, and India, with large thorium reserves, is developing thorium as a future fuel.

slides.narration: Quick check. Recall radioactivity, oxidation states and complex formation.

bullets: Lanthanoids are reactive like Ca: O₂ → Ln₂O₃; H₂ → LnH₂/LnH₃; X₂ → LnX₃; S → Ln₂S₃; N₂ → LnN; C → carbides; water → Ln(OH)₃ + H₂.
Actinoids Th–Lr fill 5f; all radioactive; transuranium elements are synthetic.
Actinoids show +3 to +7 because 5f, 6d and 7s are close in energy.
Actinoid contraction is greater; actinoids form more complexes.

visual.alt: Summary table of lanthanoid reactions

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Lanthanoids are reactive metals, like calcium, combining with oxygen, hydrogen, halogens, sulphur, nitrogen and carbon, and releasing hydrogen from water and acids, always forming tripositive compounds. The actinoids are all radioactive and show many more oxidation states, because their five f, six d and seven s levels are so close in energy.

bullets: Write products with the +3 state: Ln₂O₃, LnX₃, Ln₂S₃, LnN, Ln(OH)₃.

Present comparisons as a clear table with at least three points. And always balance the water equation: two metal atoms with six water molecules give two hydroxides and three hydrogen molecules.

sections.body_md:
**Lanthanoids:** Ce (58) to Lu (71), after La; fill 4f. General configuration $[\text{Xe}]4f^{1\text{–}14}5d^{0\text{–}1}6s^2$; 5d¹ only in La, Ce, Gd (4f⁷5d¹) and Lu (4f¹⁴5d¹). Ln³⁺: remove 6s², then 5d or one 4f electron.

**Oxidation states:** **+3** for all (lattice/hydration enthalpy repays ionisation). +4: Ce⁴⁺ (f⁰), Tb⁴⁺ (f⁷) — oxidising. +2: Eu²⁺ (f⁷), Yb²⁺ (f¹⁴), Sm²⁺ — reducing.

**Colour:** f–f transitions; f⁰ and f¹⁴ ions (La³⁺, Lu³⁺) colourless. Unpaired f electrons → paramagnetic. **Complexes:** few (large ions, 4f buried). **Alloys:** mischmetall (≈ 95% Ln, 5% Fe, traces S, C, Ca, Al) — flints, Mg alloys for shells and bullets.

sections.heading: 2. Lanthanoid contraction and its consequences
sections.body_md:
**Definition:** the steady decrease in atomic and Ln³⁺ ionic radii from La (103 pm) to Lu (86 pm). **Cause:** 4f electrons shield poorly (diffuse shape), so effective nuclear charge increases steadily.

**Consequences:** (i) 4d and 5d elements of a group have nearly equal radii (Zr 160, Hf 159 pm; Nb/Ta; Mo/W) and very similar chemistry — Zr and Hf are hard to separate; (ii) basicity of Ln(OH)₃ decreases La → Lu; (iii) lanthanoids are difficult to separate (ion exchange); (iv) 5d metals are very dense.

key_terms.definition_md: The steady decrease in size of lanthanoid atoms and Ln³⁺ ions with increasing atomic number, due to poor shielding by 4f electrons.

visual.alt: Ionic radius of the tripositive lanthanoid ions falling smoothly and steadily from about 103 picometres for lanthanum to about 86 for lutetium
visual.caption: Approximate values; the steady fall is the lanthanoid contraction.

sections.heading: 3. Chemical reactivity of lanthanoids
sections.body_md:
Strongly electropositive ($E^\circ$ ≈ −2.3 V); early members similar to calcium; reactivity falls slightly to Lu.

| Reagent | Product |
|---|---|
| O₂ (burn) | Ln₂O₃ (Ce → CeO₂) |
| H₂ (heat) | LnH₂, LnH₃ |
| X₂ (heat) | LnX₃ |
| S (heat) | Ln₂S₃ |
| N₂ (heat) | LnN |
| C (2773 K) | Ln₃C, Ln₂C₃, LnC₂ |
| H₂O | Ln(OH)₃ + H₂ |
| Dilute acid | Ln³⁺ salt + H₂ |

key_terms.definition_md: Having a strong tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions.

visual.alt: Table of selected lanthanoid reactions

sections.heading: 4. Actinoids and comparison with lanthanoids
sections.body_md:
**Actinoids:** Th (90) to Lr (103); fill 5f; $[\text{Rn}]5f^{1\text{–}14}6d^{0\text{–}1}7s^2$. All radioactive; transuranium elements synthetic.

**Oxidation states:** +3 to +7; maximum +4 (Th), +5 (Pa), +6 (U), +7 (Np, Pu), then falls; later members mainly +3. **Reason:** 5f, 6d, 7s close in energy; 5f less buried than 4f.

**Comparison:** actinoids — wider range of states, all radioactive, larger contraction, more complex formation (e.g. uranyl complexes); lanthanoids — mainly +3, only Pm radioactive, smaller contraction, fewer complexes.

key_terms.definition_md: Elements with atomic number greater than 92, all made artificially.
Decrease in size across the actinoids, greater than the lanthanoid contraction because 5f electrons shield even more poorly.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving the cause of the lanthanoid contraction as "increasing number of shells".
- Calling Ce⁴⁺ a reducing agent or Eu²⁺ an oxidising agent.
- Writing lanthanoid oxides as LnO instead of Ln₂O₃.
- Saying all lanthanoids are radioactive (only promethium).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Lanthanoid contraction (2–3 marks): definition, cause (poor 4f shielding) and consequences with examples.
- Reactivity (2 marks): correct products with +3 state and balanced equations.
- Comparison (3 marks): three distinct points, preferably in a table.

questions.stem_md: Erbium salts, used to tint glass pink, contain the Er³⁺ ion. Erbium (Z = 68) is [Xe]4f¹²6s². The configuration of Er³⁺ is:
questions.solution_md: Remove the two 6s electrons and then one 4f electron: [Xe]4f¹¹ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Ammonium cerium(IV) nitrate is used as a titrant in analytical chemistry. In these titrations the Ce⁴⁺ ion acts as:

options.text_md: a reducing agent, being oxidised to Ce⁵⁺
a catalyst that is not itself changed
a precipitating agent for the analyte
an oxidising agent, being reduced to Ce³⁺

questions.solution_md: For cerium, +3 is the most stable state, so Ce⁴⁺ readily gains an electron (E° about +1.74 V) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Gadolinium (Z = 64) has the configuration [Xe]4f⁷5d¹6s² rather than [Xe]4f⁸6s². The best reason is:

options.text_md: the half-filled 4f⁷ subshell is especially stable
the 5d subshell is lower in energy than 6s
gadolinium has no electrons in its 4f subshell
a 4f⁸ arrangement would break the 6s² pair

questions.solution_md: Keeping 4f exactly half-filled gives extra exchange stability; the eighth electron goes into 5d — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Of the aqueous ions Pr³⁺, Nd³⁺, Lu³⁺ and Er³⁺, which gives a colourless solution?
questions.solution_md: Lu³⁺ is 4f¹⁴: no f–f transition is possible — option (c). Pr³⁺ is green, Nd³⁺ lilac, Er³⁺ pink.

questions.stem_md: Which pair contains one oxidising and one reducing lanthanoid ion?
questions.solution_md: Tb⁴⁺ gains an electron to give Tb³⁺ (oxidising); Yb²⁺ loses one to give Yb³⁺ (reducing) — option (a). Eu²⁺/Sm²⁺ are both reducing, Ce⁴⁺/Tb⁴⁺ both oxidising.

questions.stem_md: Compared with Fe³⁺, the Gd³⁺ ion forms far fewer complexes. The main reason is that Gd³⁺:

options.text_md: has a smaller charge than Fe³⁺
is much larger, so its charge density is low, and its 4f orbitals are buried and not available for bonding

questions.solution_md: Large size, low charge density and shielded 4f orbitals limit complex formation — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The flint of a gas lighter is usually made of mischmetall. Mischmetall is mainly:

options.text_md: an alloy of lanthanoid metals with about 5% iron
an alloy of iron with chromium and nickel
an alloy of copper and tin

questions.solution_md: About 95% lanthanoid metals and 5% iron with traces of S, C, Ca and Al — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Every lanthanoid, from cerium to lutetium, forms compounds in the +3 oxidation state.

**Reason (R):** The high lattice and hydration enthalpies of the small Ln³⁺ ion compensate for the energy needed to remove three electrons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the energy balance in R explains why +3 is so common — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Aqueous solutions of lutetium(III) salts are coloured.

**Reason (R):** The Lu³⁺ ion has a completely filled 4f subshell.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.solution_md: A is false: with 4f¹⁴ there is no f–f transition, so Lu³⁺ is colourless. R is true — option (d).

questions.solution_md: True. Tb (4f⁹6s²) losing four electrons gives 4f⁷.

questions.stem_md: Cerium(IV) oxide, CeO₂, is used to polish glass. In the Ce⁴⁺ ion of this oxide, the 4f subshell contains ___ electrons.
questions.solution_md: Ce [Xe]4f¹5d¹6s² loses four electrons: Ce⁴⁺ is [Xe]4f⁰, **zero** f electrons.

questions.stem_md: Match each lanthanoid ion with its 4f configuration.
questions.solution_md: Ce⁴⁺ 4f⁰; Eu²⁺ 4f⁷; Yb²⁺ 4f¹⁴; Nd³⁺ 4f³.

questions.stem_md: Gadolinium(III) compounds are used as MRI contrast agents because Gd³⁺ (4f⁷) is strongly paramagnetic. Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of Gd³⁺, in BM.
questions.solution_md: 4f⁷: seven unpaired electrons, $n = 7$. $\mu = \sqrt{7 \times 9} = \sqrt{63} \approx 7.94\ \text{BM}$.

questions.stem_md: Write the electronic configurations of cerium (Z = 58), Ce³⁺ and Ce⁴⁺. Which of the two ions has a noble-gas configuration?

answer.model_answer_md: Ce: [Xe]4f¹5d¹6s². Ce³⁺: [Xe]4f¹. Ce⁴⁺: [Xe]4f⁰, i.e. the configuration of xenon. Ce⁴⁺ has the noble-gas configuration.

questions.solution_md: Ce 4f¹5d¹6s²; Ce³⁺ 4f¹; Ce⁴⁺ [Xe].

questions.stem_md: Some lanthanoids, such as europium and cerium, also form +2 or +4 ions. Explain why +3 is nevertheless the characteristic oxidation state of the lanthanoids.

answer.model_answer_md: Removing the two 6s electrons and one 4f (or 5d) electron needs energy, but the small, highly charged Ln³⁺ ion has large lattice and hydration enthalpies that more than repay it. Further ionisation would remove a deeper 4f electron, which is not repaid. Hence +3 is the most stable state; +2 and +4 ions tend to return to +3.

questions.solution_md: Energy balance favours Ln³⁺.

questions.stem_md: Aqueous neodymium(III) nitrate is lilac, but lanthanum(III) nitrate solution is colourless. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Nd³⁺ is 4f³: its f electrons can absorb certain wavelengths of visible light and move between 4f levels (f–f transitions), so the complementary lilac colour is seen. La³⁺ is 4f⁰: with no f electrons there is no f–f transition, so no visible light is absorbed.

questions.solution_md: Nd³⁺ 4f³ f–f transitions; La³⁺ 4f⁰.

questions.stem_md: Samarium, europium and ytterbium form Ln²⁺ ions, while cerium and terbium form Ln⁴⁺ ions. Using configurations, explain these states and say whether each kind of ion is oxidising or reducing. (Z: Ce 58, Sm 62, Eu 63, Tb 65, Yb 70)

answer.model_answer_md: Eu²⁺ is 4f⁷ (half-filled) and Yb²⁺ is 4f¹⁴ (full); Sm²⁺ is 4f⁶, close to half-filled. These configurations stabilise +2, but +3 is still more stable, so the Ln²⁺ ions lose an electron easily: they are reducing agents. Ce⁴⁺ is 4f⁰ (empty) and Tb⁴⁺ is 4f⁷ (half-filled); these configurations allow +4, but as +3 is more stable the Ln⁴⁺ ions gain an electron: they are oxidising agents.

questions.solution_md: Ln²⁺ (f⁷, f¹⁴, near f⁷) reducing; Ln⁴⁺ (f⁰, f⁷) oxidising.

questions.stem_md: What is mischmetall? Give its approximate composition and two uses, and suggest why lanthanoid metals form such alloys readily.

answer.model_answer_md: Mischmetall is an alloy of lanthanoid metals (about 95%, mainly Ce and La) with about 5% iron and traces of sulphur, carbon, calcium and aluminium. Uses: flints for lighters and toys; in magnesium-based alloys for bullets, shells and light parts. The lanthanoid atoms are of very similar size and metallic character, so they mix freely in the metallic lattice.

questions.solution_md: 95% Ln + 5% Fe; flints; Mg alloys; similar atomic size.

questions.stem_md: In the series La(OH)₃, Nd(OH)₃, Gd(OH)₃ and Yb(OH)₃, the basic strength:

options.text_md: increases from La(OH)₃ to Yb(OH)₃ because the nuclear charge increases
is the same for all four because all are +3 hydroxides
decreases from La(OH)₃ to Yb(OH)₃ because the Ln³⁺ ion becomes smaller
is highest for Gd(OH)₃ because Gd³⁺ is 4f⁷

questions.solution_md: Smaller Ln³⁺ polarises OH⁻ more, giving a more covalent Ln–OH bond and a weaker base — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The radius of the Ln³⁺ ion falls from 103 pm for La³⁺ to 86 pm for Lu³⁺. This happens because:

options.text_md: a new electron shell is added at each step
the number of neutrons decreases across the series
4f electrons shield the outer electrons poorly from the increasing nuclear charge

questions.solution_md: Poor shielding by the diffuse 4f orbitals lets effective nuclear charge rise steadily — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Niobium (Z = 41) and tantalum (Z = 73) have almost identical atomic radii, about 146 pm. This is because:

options.text_md: the lanthanoid contraction cancels the increase in size expected for tantalum
niobium and tantalum have the same number of electrons
tantalum has fewer electron shells than niobium

questions.solution_md: Tantalum follows the lanthanoids; their contraction offsets the extra shell — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Hafnium (13.3 g cm⁻³) is about twice as dense as zirconium (6.5 g cm⁻³). The best explanation is:

options.text_md: hafnium atoms are much smaller than zirconium atoms
hafnium has a much larger atomic radius
the two atoms are almost the same size, but hafnium is nearly twice as heavy
zirconium has more neutrons than hafnium

questions.solution_md: Same volume (lanthanoid contraction), atomic mass 178.5 vs 91.2 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Separating the individual lanthanoids present in monazite sand is difficult mainly because:

options.text_md: their ions have the same +3 charge and very similar sizes, so their properties are nearly identical

questions.solution_md: The lanthanoid contraction is gradual, so neighbouring Ln³⁺ ions are almost the same size — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The 5d metals osmium and iridium are among the densest elements known.

**Reason (R):** The lanthanoid contraction makes 5d atoms about the same size as the 4d atoms above them, while their masses are much larger.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; similar volume with much greater mass gives the very high density — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The lanthanoid contraction occurs because each additional electron across the series enters the 6s subshell.
questions.solution_md: False. The electrons enter the 4f subshell, which shields poorly.

questions.stem_md: Individual lanthanoids are separated on an industrial scale by the ___ exchange method.
questions.solution_md: The **ion** exchange method (or repeated fractional crystallisation).

questions.stem_md: The ionic radius of La³⁺ is $103\ \text{pm}$ and that of Lu³⁺ is $86\ \text{pm}$. Calculate the percentage decrease in radius from La³⁺ to Lu³⁺.
questions.solution_md: Decrease $= 103 - 86 = 17\ \text{pm}$. Percentage $= 17 \div 103 \times 100 \approx 16.5\%$.

questions.stem_md: Assume zirconium and hafnium atoms have the same volume and the same crystal structure. The density of zirconium is $6.51\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$; atomic masses: Zr $91.2$, Hf $178.5$. Estimate the density of hafnium.
questions.solution_md: Same volume, so density is proportional to atomic mass: $\rho_\text{Hf} = 6.51 \times 178.5 \div 91.2 \approx 12.74\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$ (the measured value, 13.3, is close).

questions.stem_md: Zirconium and hafnium occur together in the mineral zircon and are very hard to separate. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Hafnium follows the lanthanoids. The lanthanoid contraction cancels the increase in size expected from the extra shell, so Hf (159 pm) and Zr (160 pm) have almost the same radius and the same valence configuration. Their chemical properties are therefore almost identical, so they occur together and are hard to separate.

questions.solution_md: Lanthanoid contraction: same size, same chemistry.

questions.stem_md: Lutetium(III) hydroxide is a weaker base than lanthanum(III) hydroxide. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Because of the lanthanoid contraction, Lu³⁺ (86 pm) is smaller than La³⁺ (103 pm). The smaller ion has a higher charge density and polarises the hydroxide ion more, so the Lu–OH bond is more covalent and releases OH⁻ less readily. Hence Lu(OH)₃ is less basic.

questions.solution_md: Smaller Lu³⁺; more covalent bond.

questions.stem_md: The ionic radii of La³⁺, Gd³⁺ and Lu³⁺ are 103, 94 and 86 pm. (a) Calculate the average decrease in radius per unit increase in atomic number from La³⁺ (Z = 57) to Lu³⁺ (Z = 71). (b) Explain why the decrease per step is so small. (c) State one consequence of this decrease for the third transition series.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Average decrease $= (103 - 86) \div (71 - 57) = 17 \div 14 \approx 1.2$ pm per element. (b) Each step adds one proton and one 4f electron. The 4f electron shields the outer electrons only partly (poorly), so the effective nuclear charge rises a little each time and the size falls slowly but steadily. (c) 5d elements are almost the same size as the 4d elements above them (Zr ≈ Hf), so their chemistry is very similar.

questions.solution_md: About 1.2 pm per element; partial 4f shielding; Zr ≈ Hf.

questions.stem_md: Molybdenum (atomic mass 95.9) and tungsten (atomic mass 183.8) have almost the same atomic radius. Using the lanthanoid contraction, explain (a) their similar radii, (b) the much higher density of tungsten, and (c) their similar chemistry.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Tungsten comes after the fourteen lanthanoids; the poor shielding by 4f electrons increases the effective nuclear charge enough to cancel the extra shell, so W is no larger than Mo. (b) With nearly the same atomic volume but almost twice the mass, tungsten is much denser (about 19.3 vs 10.2 g cm⁻³). (c) Same size and same valence configuration give very similar chemical properties.

questions.solution_md: Contraction; same volume, more mass; similar chemistry.

questions.stem_md: When neodymium metal is heated in nitrogen, the product formed is:
questions.solution_md: Lanthanoids combine with nitrogen on heating to give LnN, with Ln in the +3 state — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Lanthanum metal is added to hot water. The products are:
questions.solution_md: 2La + 6H₂O → 2La(OH)₃ + 3H₂ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Heating a lanthanoid metal with carbon at about 2773 K gives:

options.text_md: carbides such as LnC₂, Ln₂C₃ and Ln₃C
no reaction, as carbon is inert

questions.solution_md: Lanthanoids form carbides at high temperature — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Most lanthanoids burn in oxygen to give oxides of formula Ln₂O₃. Cerium, however, burns to give:
questions.solution_md: Cerium forms the +4 oxide CeO₂ (4f⁰) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In their reactions with water, acids and non-metals, the early lanthanoids such as lanthanum and cerium behave most like:
questions.solution_md: They are highly electropositive (E° about −2.3 V), like calcium — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Samarium metal is heated with sulphur. The formula of the sulphide formed is:
questions.solution_md: Sm³⁺ and S²⁻ combine in the ratio 2 : 3 — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lanthanoid metals liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid.

**Reason (R):** Lanthanoids form hydrides of formula LnH₂ and LnH₃ when heated with hydrogen.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the formation of hydrides does not explain the reaction with acid (which is due to the metals being strongly electropositive) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Cerium metal dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid with the evolution of hydrogen.
questions.solution_md: True. 2Ce + 6HCl → 2CeCl₃ + 3H₂.

questions.stem_md: Heating holmium with sulphur gives the sulphide Ho₂S₃, in which holmium is in the +___ oxidation state.
questions.solution_md: Ho₂S₃: 2x = 6, so holmium is **+3**.

questions.stem_md: Match each reaction of dysprosium metal with its product.
questions.solution_md: Oxygen → Dy₂O₃; chlorine → DyCl₃; nitrogen → DyN; water → Dy(OH)₃ + H₂.

questions.stem_md: $2.778\ \text{g}$ of lanthanum is burnt completely in oxygen: $\ce{4La + 3O2 -> 2La2O3}$. Calculate the mass of lanthanum oxide formed. (La = 138.9, O = 16.0)

marking_scheme.step: Moles of La and of oxide

questions.stem_md: $0.020\ \text{mol}$ of cerium reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid: $\ce{2Ce + 6HCl -> 2CeCl3 + 3H2}$. Calculate the volume of hydrogen formed at STP, in litres. (Molar volume $22.4\ \text{L}$)
Write balanced equations for the reaction of (a) lanthanum with water and (b) gadolinium with nitrogen on heating.
questions.solution_md: Two balanced equations.

questions.stem_md: What is formed when a lanthanoid metal such as cerium is heated (a) with carbon at about 2773 K, and (b) with hydrogen?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Carbides of formula Ln₃C, Ln₂C₃ and LnC₂ (e.g. CeC₂). (b) Hydrides LnH₂ and LnH₃ (e.g. CeH₃).

questions.solution_md: Carbides; hydrides.

questions.stem_md: Write balanced equations for: (a) europium burning in oxygen to give the +3 oxide; (b) terbium heated with bromine; (c) lutetium dissolving in dilute sulphuric acid.
questions.solution_md: Three balanced equations.

questions.stem_md: Compare the reactivity of the lanthanoids with that of calcium. In your answer, (a) give the reason for their high reactivity, (b) state how reactivity changes from lanthanum to lutetium, and (c) give one equation showing a calcium-like reaction.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) They are strongly electropositive metals with $E^\circ_{\ce{Ln^3+/Ln}}$ about −2.3 V, close to that of calcium, so they lose electrons readily. (b) Reactivity decreases slightly from La to Lu as the atoms become smaller (lanthanoid contraction) and hold their electrons more firmly. (c) $\ce{2La + 6H2O -> 2La(OH)3 + 3H2}$, like $\ce{Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2}$.

questions.solution_md: Electropositive; decreases slightly; reaction with water.

questions.stem_md: Plutonium forms compounds in every oxidation state from +3 to +7. Which feature of its electronic structure makes this possible?

options.text_md: Its 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are close in energy, so varying numbers of electrons can be used in bonding
It has no electrons in its 5f subshell

questions.solution_md: Close 5f/6d/7s energies and less buried 5f orbitals allow many electrons to be used — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which property is shown by every actinoid but by only one lanthanoid?

options.text_md: Formation of compounds in the +3 state

questions.solution_md: All actinoids are radioactive; among lanthanoids only promethium is — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Thorium dioxide, ThO₂, was once used in gas lamp mantles. The oxidation state of thorium in ThO₂ is:
questions.solution_md: x + 2(−2) = 0, so x = +4 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Americium, used in household smoke detectors, is called a transuranium element because:

options.text_md: its atomic number is greater than that of uranium and it is made artificially
it is extracted from uranium ores
it has the same atomic number as uranium

questions.solution_md: Elements with Z > 92 are transuranium elements, all synthetic — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The contraction in size across the actinoid series is greater than that across the lanthanoids. This is because:

options.text_md: actinoids have fewer electrons than lanthanoids
5f electrons are closer to the nucleus than 4f electrons
5f electrons shield the outer electrons even more poorly than 4f electrons

questions.solution_md: Poorer shielding by 5f electrons gives a larger increase in effective nuclear charge — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The ground-state electronic configuration of thorium (Z = 90), the first actinoid, is:
questions.solution_md: Thorium has no 5f electrons in its ground state: [Rn]6d²7s² — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The chemistry of elements such as einsteinium and fermium is far less known than that of the lanthanoids mainly because:

options.text_md: they are gases at room temperature
they do not form any compounds
they are radioactive, have short half-lives and are available only in tiny amounts
they are too unreactive to study

questions.solution_md: Short half-lives and tiny quantities make heavy actinoids hard to study — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Actinoids form complexes more readily than lanthanoids.

**Reason (R):** All actinoid ions have a completely filled 5f subshell.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true (higher charge density, 5f orbitals available). R is false: actinoid ions have partly filled 5f subshells — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? All the actinoids beyond uranium occur naturally in large amounts in uranium ores.
questions.solution_md: False. Transuranium elements are made artificially (only traces of Np and Pu occur naturally).

questions.stem_md: The highest oxidation state shown by neptunium and plutonium is +___.
Calculate the oxidation state of uranium in sodium diuranate, Na₂U₂O₇ (a form of "yellowcake").
Why are the transuranium elements made artificially? Name one such element and give one of its uses.

answer.model_answer_md: Their isotopes are radioactive with half-lives short compared with the age of the Earth, so any formed originally have decayed; they are made in nuclear reactors or accelerators by bombarding heavier nuclei. Example: plutonium, used as nuclear fuel (or americium in smoke detectors).

questions.solution_md: Short half-lives; plutonium fuel.

questions.stem_md: Uranium shows oxidation states +3, +4, +5 and +6, whereas lanthanoids rarely go beyond +3. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: In uranium the 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are very close in energy, and 5f orbitals extend further from the nucleus than 4f orbitals, so different numbers of these electrons can be used in bonding (up to all six). In lanthanoids the 4f electrons are buried and much lower in energy, so only three electrons are usually lost.

questions.solution_md: Close 5f/6d/7s energies; 4f buried.

questions.stem_md: Compare lanthanoids and actinoids with respect to (a) the size of the contraction across each series, (b) their occurrence in nature, and (c) the basic character of their oxides.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Both contract, but the actinoid contraction is greater because 5f electrons shield more poorly than 4f. (b) Lanthanoids occur naturally (e.g. in monazite), except promethium; among actinoids only thorium and uranium occur in significant amounts — the rest are made artificially. (c) Lanthanoid oxides are basic; actinoid oxides are less basic (and some actinoids in high states form amphoteric or acidic oxides).

questions.solution_md: Contraction; occurrence; basicity.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the oxidation state of uranium in (a) uranium tetrafluoride, UF₄, (b) uranium trioxide, UO₃, and (c) the uranyl ion, UO₂²⁺. What does the result show about actinoids compared with lanthanoids?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) x + 4(−1) = 0: +4. (b) x + 3(−2) = 0: +6. (c) x + 2(−2) = +2: +6. Uranium readily shows +4 and +6, whereas lanthanoids are mainly +3 and never exceed +4; actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states.

questions.solution_md: +4; +6; +6; wider range.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the electronic configurations of gadolinium (Z = 64) and of the Gd³⁺ ion. [1½]

(b) Explain why +3 is the most stable oxidation state of the lanthanoids, and why Ce⁴⁺ is an oxidising agent while Yb²⁺ is a reducing agent. [2]

(c) Explain why Nd³⁺ salts are coloured but Lu³⁺ salts are colourless. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Gd: [Xe]4f⁷5d¹6s². Gd³⁺: [Xe]4f⁷.

(b) The energy needed to remove three electrons is repaid by the large lattice and hydration enthalpies of the small Ln³⁺ ion, so +3 is the most stable state. Ce⁴⁺ (4f⁰) gains an electron to return to +3, so it is oxidising. Yb²⁺ (4f¹⁴) loses an electron to reach +3, so it is reducing.

(c) Nd³⁺ (4f³) has partly filled f orbitals; f–f transitions absorb visible light and the complementary colour is seen. Lu³⁺ (4f¹⁴) has a full subshell, so no f–f transition is possible.

questions.solution_md: Gd 4f⁷5d¹6s²; +3 stability; Ce⁴⁺ oxidising, Yb²⁺ reducing; f–f transitions.

questions.stem_md:
(a) The Ln³⁺ radius falls from 103 pm (La³⁺) to 86 pm (Lu³⁺). Name this effect and explain its cause. [2]

(b) Use it to explain (i) the very similar chemistry of niobium and tantalum, and (ii) the decrease in basic strength from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃. [2]

(c) Why are individual lanthanoids difficult to separate, and which method is used? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The lanthanoid contraction. Across the series each added electron enters the 4f subshell; 4f orbitals are diffuse and shield the outer electrons poorly, so the effective nuclear charge increases steadily and the atoms and ions shrink.

(b) (i) Tantalum comes after the lanthanoids; the contraction cancels the expected increase in size, so Nb and Ta have almost the same radius and very similar chemistry. (ii) The Ln³⁺ ion becomes smaller from La to Lu, polarises OH⁻ more and forms a more covalent Ln–OH bond, so the hydroxide becomes less basic.

(c) Neighbouring lanthanoids have the same +3 charge and almost the same size, so their properties are nearly identical; they are separated by ion exchange (or fractional crystallisation).

questions.solution_md: Lanthanoid contraction; Nb ≈ Ta; basicity; ion exchange.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write balanced equations for the reactions of holmium with (i) oxygen, (ii) chlorine, (iii) nitrogen and (iv) water. [2]

(b) Calculate the mass of holmium(III) oxide formed when 3.298 g of holmium burns completely in oxygen. (Ho = 164.9, O = 16.0) [2]

(c) Why does reactivity decrease slightly from lanthanum to lutetium? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) $\ce{4Ho + 3O2 -> 2Ho2O3}$; (ii) $\ce{2Ho + 3Cl2 -> 2HoCl3}$; (iii) $\ce{2Ho + N2 -> 2HoN}$; (iv) $\ce{2Ho + 6H2O -> 2Ho(OH)3 + 3H2}$.

(b) $n(\text{Ho}) = 3.298 \div 164.9 = 0.0200\ \text{mol}$, so $n(\text{Ho}_2\text{O}_3) = 0.0100\ \text{mol}$. $M = 2 \times 164.9 + 48.0 = 377.8$. Mass $= 0.0100 \times 377.8 \approx 3.78\ \text{g}$.

(c) The atoms become smaller (lanthanoid contraction) and the effective nuclear charge increases, so the outer electrons are held more firmly and lost less readily.

questions.solution_md: Four equations; about 3.78 g; contraction.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Smaller atoms hold electrons more firmly

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the electronic configurations of thorium (Z = 90) and uranium (Z = 92). Why are the actinoids called 5f elements? [1½]

(b) Give the oxidation state of uranium in UF₆, UO₂²⁺ and U⁴⁺, and explain why actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids. [2]

(c) Give two reasons why the chemistry of the actinoids is harder to study than that of the lanthanoids. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Th: [Rn]6d²7s²; U: [Rn]5f³6d¹7s². Across the series the differentiating electrons enter the 5f subshell, so they are called 5f elements (even though thorium itself has no 5f electron in its ground state).

(b) UF₆: +6; UO₂²⁺: +6; U⁴⁺: +4. The 5f, 6d and 7s levels are close in energy and 5f orbitals are less deeply buried than 4f, so a variable number of electrons can take part in bonding.

(c) All actinoids are radioactive (hazardous, need special handling); many have short half-lives and are available only in tiny amounts; their wide range of oxidation states makes their chemistry complicated.

questions.solution_md: Configurations; +6, +6, +4; close energies; radioactivity and scarcity.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Give four differences between the lanthanoids and the actinoids in a table. [2]

(b) Explain why the actinoid contraction is greater than the lanthanoid contraction. [1½]

(c) Give one important use each of mischmetall, neodymium and uranium. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Lanthanoids: 4f filled; mainly +3, at most +4; only Pm radioactive; fewer complexes; basic oxides. Actinoids: 5f filled; +3 to +7; all radioactive; more complexes; less basic oxides.

(b) 5f orbitals are more diffuse than 4f orbitals and shield the outer electrons even more poorly, so the effective nuclear charge increases more sharply from one element to the next.

(c) Mischmetall: lighter flints (or Mg alloys for shells). Neodymium: powerful permanent magnets (Nd₂Fe₁₄B) in motors. Uranium: nuclear fuel.

questions.solution_md: Four differences; poorer 5f shielding; uses.
